echoes.note: Epaenetus is called 'the first fruits (aparche) of Achaia.' The metaphor draws on the cultic offering of firstfruits — the first and best of the harvest consecrated to God (Exodus 23:19; Deuteronomy 26:1-11). The link is purely conceptual reuse of an offering-term as a name for the first convert; no verbal borrowing, so faint and disputed.

'The God of peace will quickly crush Satan under your feet' (16:20) alludes to the protoevangelium: 'he shall bruise/crush your head' addressed to the serpent. The verb (crush/bruise) plus the bodily image (head/feet, enemy trodden underfoot) reactivates Genesis 3:15, with Satan now read as the serpent and the church as the seed of the woman who treads him down. Strong verbal and figural coherence; Paul universalizes the promised victory.

The image of the enemy placed 'under your feet' overlaps with the subjugation language of Psalm 8:6 ('you have put all things under his feet'), which Paul uses elsewhere for Christ's triumph. Here the dominant source is Genesis 3:15; the 'under feet' phrasing is at most a secondary, disputed resonance.

The dividers' 'smooth and flattering speech' that 'deceive the hearts of the innocent' (16:18) echoes the wisdom/psalmic indictment of smooth, flattering lips that deceive (Psalm 12:2-3; cf. Proverbs 26:28). Thematic and partly verbal but a common topos, so contested.

The deceivers who beguile 'the hearts of the innocent' with smooth speech (16:18) typologically recall the serpent who deceived by crafty words — a figure reinforced two verses later by the explicit Genesis 3:15 allusion (16:20). The serpent-as-deceiver framing is suggestive but disputed as an intended echo here.
